messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tane stood in the walk-in prep kitchen when the heavy door clicked shut behind him. The steel frame, once just another part of his nightly routine, became an inescapable trap. Two years ago, during a late shift at a downtown bistro, a supervisor had cornered him among stacked delivery crates, pinning his wrists against the stainless steel prep table. The assault was prolonged and humiliating, defined by the scent of industrial cleaner, the damp cold of the floor against his cheek, and the brutal realization that his status as a respected chef offered no protection. In the months that followed, the very environment that had once defined his competence turned hostile. The metallic scrape of a knife block, the smell of bleach on his own hands, and the muffled silence of the sealed cooler door became visceral reminders. Every time the heavy door closed, his chest tightened, and his hands instinctively wiped themselves against his apron, as if he could scrub away the memory of being overpowered. He had come to believe that his life was destroyed by the trauma. The confidence that had once guided his knife work dissolved into a quiet conviction that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. He stopped wearing his chef’s whites, finding that the uniform felt like a costume for a man who no longer existed. Instead, he began showering repeatedly, scrubbing his skin until it was raw, driven by a persistent sensation that he felt dirty or contaminated because of what happened. When colleagues asked about his sudden absence from the pass, he offered only vague excuses, unable to articulate the truth without his words fracturing. He could talk about what happened very easily, laying out the facts for his therapist in a steady, detached voice, but when he tried to hold the full picture in his mind, the pieces would slip. He could not put the memories of the event in the right order, the timeline blurring between the heavy door shutting and the final moments of the aftermath. Whenever the recollection approached its full weight, he found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, a reflexive retreat that left him breathless and isolated. The more convinced he became that his life was destroyed and that he carried an unshakable stain, the more actively his mind worked to fracture the event. His negative appraisals directly dictated his memory processing; the conviction that he was ruined made the trauma too dangerous to face completely. As he told himself he was no longer capable of functioning, his mental focus narrowed to the threat of another memory, tightening the loop that kept the past locked in disjointed fragments. He avoided the kitchen entirely, taking a quiet inventory job at a warehouse instead, but the avoidance only deepened the sense of contamination. Every day spent in isolation reinforced the appraisal that he was broken, and that appraisal, in turn, demanded he push the memory away before it could surface. The cycle tightened over months, a quiet erosion where the belief of ruin drove the fragmentation, and the fragmentation guaranteed he would never finish processing what occurred. Now, at forty-five, Tane sits in the intake office, the weight of two years pressing down on his shoulders. His divorce had already strained his support network, and the silence that followed his resignation from the kitchen left him entirely alone. What finally brought him to seek help was the morning he found himself unable to leave his apartment, convinced that stepping outside would expose the contamination he was certain clung to his skin. He is most afraid that the appraisal of ruin is permanent, that the man he was will never return, but he is also desperately hoping that someone can help him remember the event without it destroying him again. He wants to believe he can step back into a kitchen without the heavy door sealing shut around him, and he is willing to do whatever it takes to find that possibility.
